query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, controlled annealing induces diffusion‐driven precipitation of stable Mg-rich intermetallic phases from a supersaturated solid solution. This phase evolution alters local elemental distributions such that a more uniform, less galvanically active microstructure forms that promotes the development of an adherent, protective oxide layer during high-temperature exposure, thereby improving both corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An induction‐cast alloy with density below 6 g/cm3 exhibiting a supersaturated solid-solution matrix with dispersed, non-equilibrium intermetallic seeds
generation.intervention: Controlled heat treatment (annealing) designed to promote diffusion-driven precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases
generation.conditions: Processing constrained to alloys with density <6 g/cm3; heat treatment parameters (temperature and duration) chosen to allow partial phase separation without bulk melting; subsequent testing in corrosive environments (e.g., 0.1 M NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 700–900°C)
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitated Mg-rich intermetallic phases that adjust local elemental partitioning and reduce micro-galvanic sites, thus mediating the formation of a uniform, passivating oxide layer
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment enables diffusion, driving the precipitation of stable intermetallic compounds from the originally supersaturated matrix. This transformation changes the spatial distribution of reactive elements—reducing localized differences that otherwise promote galvanic corrosion—and facilitates the development of an oxide film that is more adherent and protective during high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the heat-treated alloy will show lower corrosion current densities, higher corrosion potentials, and formation of a more uniform, adherent oxide scale under high-temperature oxidation tests, thereby indicating enhanced corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast non-equilibrium structure with a largely homogeneous supersaturated solid solution and less defined intermetallic precipitates
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to lightweight, Mg-containing high-entropy alloys processed under conditions where diffusion is thermally activated (without complete equilibration) and the density remains below 6 g/cm3; it assumes that constituent property differences are sufficient to drive stable intermetallic formation.
generation.uncertainty: The specific types, volume fractions, and spatial distributions of the Mg-rich intermetallic phases may vary with slight compositional shifts and processing parameters, which might affect the quantification of corrosion/oxidation improvements; additional alloy-specific factors might also play a role.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples via induction melting to achieve the non-equilibrium as-cast state. Subject one set to a controlled annealing treatment designed to induce intermetallic precipitation. Expose both sets to standardized corrosion (e.g., immersion in 0.1 M NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation (e.g., isothermal treatment at 800°C) tests.
measurements: Electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization) to record corrosion potential and current density
Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM/EDS) to assess intermetallic phase distribution and morphologies
Oxidation tests (e.g., weight gain measurement, XPS, and oxide scale imaging) to evaluate oxide film uniformity and adhesion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated sample does not display a statistically significant improvement in corrosion and oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast baseline or if microstructural analysis does not reveal a substantial precipitation of stable intermetallic phases altering elemental partitioning, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRecently, the design of lightweight high entropy alloys (HEAs) with a mass density lower than 5 g/cm3 has attracted much research interest in structural materials. We applied a first principles-based high-throughput method to design lightweight HEAs in single solid-solution phase. Three lightweight quinary HEA families were studied: AlBeMgTiLi, AlBeMgTiSi and AlBeMgTiCu. By comprehensively exploring their entire compositional spaces, we identified the most promising compositions according to the following design criteria: the highest stability, lowest mass density, largest elastic modulus and specific stiffness, along with highest Pugh’s ratio. We found that HEAs with the topmost compositions exhibit a negative formation energy, a low density and high specific Young’s modulus, but a low Pugh’s ratio. Importantly, we show that the most stable composition, Al0.31Be0.15Mg0.14Ti0.05Si0.35 is energetically more stable than its metallic compounds and it significantly outperforms the current lightweight engineering alloys such as the 7075 Al alloy. This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. The selected Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 and Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8 alloys were analysed for structural behavior by CALPHAD, solidification and kinetics simulations. Phase diagrams showed the formation of a multiphase structure with preponderant solid solutions. Intermetallic compound-based phases were found at lower concentrations but still significantly higher than in the conventional aluminum alloys. Two invariant transformations were indicated for Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, with a BCC-A2 phase stable between 316–488 °C. The influence of the elements on the structural evolution were similar with the results obtained from semiempirical criteria calculations. The non-equilibrium solidification simulation discussed the order of which the phases are solidifying in normal casting conditions. The soft FCC phase is stabilizing first in the Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, while intermetallic compound phases Mg2Si and Al9Mn2Si are forming first in the Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8 alloy.
